turns.text: What do you remember about your very first day arriving in Beidahuang after leaving Shanghai? What did you see, smell, and feel as you stepped off the train or bus?

The first thing I noticed was the wind—sharp and raw, colder than anything I’d felt in Shanghai. My city had always been crowded, noisy, thick with cooking smells and the hum of trams, but here the air was empty and biting, carrying only the faint scent of earth and something metallic. The train platform was rough, uneven ground, not the stone I was used to. I remember mud clinging to my shoes, heavy and sticky, making every step feel uncertain. The sky stretched out in a colorless sheet, pressing down. There were no buildings crowding close, just a few low sheds and a line of unfamiliar faces, all watching us with the same wary curiosity.

My hands ached from gripping my suitcase. I felt small. The others in my group tried to look brave, but I saw their eyes darting, searching for something familiar. My stomach was tight with hunger and nerves. The instructions from the loudspeaker echoed in my head, but already the words felt far away, replaced by the sound of boots squelching in mud and the distant calls of birds I didn’t recognize. I remember thinking, this isn’t a place for people, not really. It felt like the world had emptied out, and we were the last ones left.

It sounds like the landscape itself made you feel exposed and unsettled, almost as if you’d landed on another planet. You mentioned the unfamiliar faces watching you—what was your first interaction like with the local people or the other sent-down youth who had arrived before you?

The first real interaction happened as we were herded toward the dormitory. Some of the local workers stood off to the side, arms crossed, faces unreadable. One of them, older and sunburned, called out something in a thick accent I barely understood. I remember the way his eyes flicked over our clothes—our city jackets, our shoes still clean except for the new mud. He didn’t smile. None of them did.

Inside the dorm, a few sent-down youth who’d arrived earlier were already unpacking. Their voices were quieter, their hair shaggier, and their hands looked rough. One girl glanced up, met my eyes, and looked away. I tried to ask where to put my bag, but she just shrugged and kept folding her quilt. It wasn’t unkind, just tired. I realized then that there was a gulf between those who’d been here a while and us newcomers—like they’d crossed a river we hadn’t touched yet.

That night, someone loaned me an extra blanket without saying a word. It smelled of smoke and something sour, but I was grateful. We all lay there, listening to the wind rattle the windowpanes, each of us pretending to be asleep. I felt like I was intruding on a world that didn’t want me.

The silence in that room pressed heavier than the cold. I kept thinking how, back home, even strangers would ask questions or make jokes to break the ice, but here, every word seemed like a risk. I watched how the others moved—quick, careful, always watching the door. Even the way they ate was different: hunched over, guarding their bowls, as if food might be taken away. That first meal, I tasted more salt from my own sweat than from the soup.

I tried to make small talk, but it fell flat. The older ones had learned not to trust too easily. They’d seen newcomers come and go, some breaking down, some trying to run, some just fading into the routine. I remember lying awake, feeling the straw mattress prick my skin, wondering how long it would take before I became like them—tough on the outside, silent on the inside. I missed Shanghai’s noise, the way the city never let you feel alone, even when you wanted to be. Here, loneliness was the air we breathed.

Your description of the meal, especially tasting more salt from your sweat than from the soup, makes the hardship feel physical and immediate. When you think back to those early meals, was there ever a moment when food brought you comfort or connection, even briefly, with someone else in the dorm?

Once, maybe a week or so after I arrived, I saw one of the older boys slip a piece of fried dough from his pocket and break it in half. He didn’t say anything, just nudged it across the table with his elbow as if it was nothing. I hesitated, but the smell—greasy, sweet, familiar—made my mouth water. I took it and nodded, and for a moment the silence between us changed. We chewed slowly, pretending not to notice each other, but I felt a kind of warmth I hadn’t felt since leaving home.

After that, sometimes someone would pass around a handful of sunflower seeds, or a lump of sugar saved from a care package. There was never enough to fill your stomach, but sharing made it taste better. It was like a secret language—no words, just small gestures that said, I see you, I know what you’re feeling. Those moments didn’t erase the hunger, but they made it less lonely.

Hunger made every bite precious, but it was the sharing that stayed with me. Sometimes, in the evenings after the work bell, we’d sit on the edge of our beds and someone would bring out a steamed bun, hard as stone from the cold. We’d tear it into uneven pieces and pass them around, careful not to let the crumbs fall. No one spoke, but in the way fingers brushed or eyes met, I felt less like a stranger. 

There was a girl who once traded me a sliver of preserved plum for a story about Shanghai. I told her about the lanterns at New Year, how the city glowed red and gold, and for a few minutes, our world grew bigger than the dorm walls. Food was never just food—it was a way to remember who we were before, and to remind each other that we hadn’t disappeared completely into the mud and cold. Those small exchanges were the closest thing we had to kindness.

I can see how those trades and quiet moments of sharing helped you hold onto your sense of self, even when everything else felt stripped away. When you told stories about Shanghai, did you ever worry that remembering home too vividly would make things harder, or did it help you survive?

Both, in a way. Some nights, after telling a story, I’d lie awake and ache for the city—the smell of fried scallion pancakes on the street, the way rain sounded on the old roof tiles, even the crowded buses. Remembering made the distance sharper. But if I tried to shut it out completely, I felt emptier, like I was dissolving into the endless fields. 

Sometimes I saw it in the others, too. If someone got a letter from home, they’d read it over and over, then tuck it away and not speak for hours. We all learned not to talk about Shanghai too much, especially when work was hardest or food was scarcest. But deep down, I think holding onto those memories was what kept me from disappearing. It was a quiet rebellion: refusing to let this place erase everything I’d been. Even if it hurt, it reminded me I was still myself.

You’re right that memory could cut both ways. There were days when the ache for home felt like a fever—my mind would drift to the sound of my sisters laughing, or the heavy perfume of osmanthus in the fall, and for a moment I’d lose my grip on the present. Sometimes, I envied those who seemed to let go of the past more easily; they moved through the days with fewer sharp edges inside. But whenever I tried to forget, I felt myself growing numb, and that numbness frightened me more than the pain of missing home. 

I never spoke about this out loud, not even in whispers. It felt dangerous, as if someone might use my longing against me, or label it as weakness. The slogans on the walls demanded we “transform ourselves,” but I clung to the small details of my old life as proof that I hadn’t been fully remade. I suppose that’s why I kept telling stories, even when it left me raw. I needed to remember what sweetness was, so I’d know what I was fighting to keep inside.

It’s striking how you describe numbness as even more frightening than pain, and how memory became a quiet form of resistance. You mentioned the slogans on the walls—was there ever a moment when you felt pressured to hide or change something about yourself to fit in, and how did you handle it?

Almost every day I felt that pressure, but one memory stands out. Early on, I still spoke with a city accent, especially when I was tired or upset. One morning, after a meeting, someone mocked the way I pronounced a word, stretching out the syllables in front of everyone. Laughter followed, sharp and mean, and I felt my face burn. After that, I practiced speaking with a heavier local accent, flattening my words so I wouldn’t stand out. I stopped mentioning books I’d read or music I liked—those things marked me as “soft,” too much a city kid.

Sometimes I caught myself slouching, copying the way the older workers walked, trying to look like I belonged. But I couldn’t change everything. At night, I’d whisper poetry to myself under the covers, or trace the characters for my family’s names in the dust on my bedframe. Those were the pieces I kept hidden, small and silent, so I wouldn’t lose them. Out loud, I tried to be what was expected, but inside, I guarded those fragments fiercely.

I remember the exact sound of that laughter—how it echoed in the drafty room and seemed to stick to my skin for hours. My hands shook when I tried to eat lunch that day. Afterward, I started listening more than speaking. I watched how the others moved, how they spat on the ground or cursed under their breath, and I tried to pick up their habits like armor. I hated it, but I was afraid of being singled out again. 

Sometimes, I’d catch my reflection in the window at dusk—hair tangled, face smudged, mouth set in a line—and I’d barely recognize myself. The slogans on the walls weren’t just words; they seeped into the way people watched each other, always alert for signs of difference. I learned to keep my head down, to laugh when everyone else laughed, to nod at the right times. But when I was alone, I’d go over lines from old stories in my head, or run my fingers over the smooth stone I’d brought from home. I couldn’t let go of those small things, even if it meant hiding them like secrets. That was the only way I knew to stay whole.

The image of you tracing your family’s names in dust and holding onto a stone from home really lingers—it shows how survival sometimes depended on protecting even the smallest private rituals. Looking back now, do you think those hidden acts of self-preservation changed how you relate to trust and openness with others, even years later?
